title: A constitutive closure that still works in a flow it was not fitted to

concept.text: The innovation would be a material description that predicts stress when a complex fluid encounters a different kind of deformation or a different deformation history from those used to identify the description. Such a constitutive closure supplies the stress relation needed to turn conservation of mass and momentum into predictions of flow. The goal is to infer it from microstructure or informative flow measurements, then hold it fixed while predicting new combinations of shear, stretching and time-dependent forcing.

The relation must be frame-invariant: changing the observer's orientation or motion must not change its physical predictions. For materials with memory, it must also represent how earlier deformation changes the present material state and stress. The target is transferable prediction within explicitly stated material classes and operating ranges. Selected simulated examples already demonstrate transfer; the larger proposed advance is reliable, experimentally validated transfer across sufficiently demanding changes of kinematics and history.

significance.text: Conventional rheometry can leave different constitutive laws nearly indistinguishable under simple test conditions even though they predict substantially different behavior in mixed shear and extension. The supplied preprint describes failures to predict strong resistance to stretching in contractions from simpler characterization. A broadly validated transferable closure would address this ambiguity at the point where it matters for engineering: predicting a previously untested flow rather than reproducing a fitted rheometer response.

Conditional engineering significance: with conservation laws, suitable boundary and initial conditions, relevant material-state information and adequate numerical resolution, such a closure could make velocity, pressure and stress predictable in a withheld die, nozzle, coating flow or porous geometry. Within its demonstrated domain, this could reduce repeated calibration and geometry-specific trials in processing, printing and related applications. These are consequences of the proposed capability, not evidence that entire industries currently depend exclusively on such trials.

Interpretive analogy: the advance would move complex-fluid prediction toward the practical role that a known viscosity plays for a Newtonian fluid. The analogy has limits. A complex fluid may require evolving internal variables, several relaxation processes and a specified preparation history rather than one scalar parameter. A transferable stress law would also not by itself solve inverse molecular design, direct stress measurement or computation at processing-scale elasticity. Conditional downstream gains in material optimization and process control would depend on those additional capabilities.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central gap is identifying and validating the right constitutive structure, not simply fitting parameters more accurately. Competing laws can reproduce the same bulk measurements while responding differently to another forcing protocol. Consequently, simple-shear agreement alone does not establish an extensional prediction across competing model classes. Identification requires measurements that discriminate among relevant mechanisms, followed by tests that were not used to choose the model or its parameters. Finite observations can establish useful identification within a restricted class without uniquely determining every possible constitutive law.

Memory creates a second barrier: the internal variables must retain the aspects of deformation history that affect future stress. The reviewed preprint notes that no finite internal-state architecture spans every possible history-dependent behavior. Its demonstrations therefore leave a meaningful extension problem involving multimode relaxation, thixotropy, aging and additional memory variables. A closure that transfers for one relaxation mechanism need not transfer for a material whose structure rebuilds, ages or yields through different mechanisms.

The engineering challenge is to preserve physical constraints such as frame invariance while inferring stress behavior from partial flow observations, then carry that behavior into experimentally measured, fully three-dimensional and potentially interfacial flows. The supplied work demonstrates components of this route, including tensor-basis closures and differentiable flow solvers, but broad experimental validation remains beyond its reported synthetic demonstrations. Proposed practical development would need to distinguish constitutive error from errors in measured inputs, boundary conditions and numerical solution.

current_state.text: The strongest retained evidence in the supplied review is the preprint Learning constitutive models and rheology from partial flow measurements by A. M. Sunol and coauthors. Although the earlier research labels the work as January 2026 v2, the retained PDF and HTML identify themselves as September 2026 v4; the landing-page history records v4 on 7 September 2026. The results described here therefore belong to that later version. The supplied record identifies no journal publication for the work, so these remain preprint-reported findings.

The September version reports a differentiable solver with instantaneous and memory tensor-basis closures. A learned generalized-Newtonian viscosity transfers from a simulated constriction to a different porous geometry. More substantially, a Giesekus memory closure trained in a simulated contraction is used in an unseen lid-driven cavity without retraining, including predictions of transient conformation, an internal description of polymer deformation. This establishes reported simulated transfer beyond an instantaneous viscosity law.

The preprint also reports FENE-P and Saramito tests addressing finite extensibility and yield-stress behavior. Together with the Giesekus results, these support the ability of the framework to represent several constitutive mechanisms from velocity data. They do not establish that every mechanism, material or deformation history transfers successfully. The earlier characterization of the available work as only inelastic or shear-dominated, with viscoelasticity still entirely unfinished, does not describe the retained September version.

These are bounded demonstrations using synthetic flow data. Multimode relaxation, thixotropy, aging, additional memory variables, interfacial multiphase flow, fully three-dimensional flows and experimental flow-data applications remain extensions in the supplied review's account. Both full-text extractions are truncated, with the PDF extraction ending during page 27. The review supports the reported results through retained text; it does not supply an independent assessment of plotted figures or a complete reading of every part of the paper. The supplied search record also does not establish comprehensive coverage of subsequent developments.

The earlier research additionally cites a British Society of Rheology review dated 30 September 2026 and an Applied Physics Letters editorial dated 19 October 2026 as descriptions of continuing constitutive-model challenges. Neither has retained text in the supplied source record. Their attributed statements about a unified framework, frame invariance and flow-history generalization therefore cannot serve as independently checked findings here. In particular, the research's narrower assertion that wormlike-micelle fluids lack one rheological equation predicting transients, banding and turbulence together remains an unresolved contextual claim. The absence of retained evidence does not establish that assertion is false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed experimental benchmark: use at least three materially different fluids—an entangled polymer solution or melt, a yield-stress gel and a thixotropic suspension. For each, withhold all measurements from a specified inhomogeneous test flow containing both shear and extension. Infer the material's closure from microstructure or other flows, freeze the closure and its parameters, and predict the withheld velocity field and pressure drop without refitting. The three-fluid choice is a proposed breadth test, not an established community standard.
completion_criteria.label: Frozen closures predict withheld velocity and pressure across three fluids

completion_criteria.text: Proposed acceptance conditions: pre-register the material preparation, operating ranges, boundary and initial conditions, measurement uncertainty, error metrics and numerical acceptance thresholds. Where an elasticity-driven excess pressure is experimentally distinguishable from zero, require the prediction to recover its sign relative to an explicitly defined reference as well as its magnitude within the chosen tolerance. This is a proposed diagnostic; the supplied evidence does not establish the earlier specific claim that shear-fitted Boger-fluid models predict the wrong pressure sign.
completion_criteria.label: Pre-registered criteria require distinguishable excess-pressure sign and magnitude accuracy

completion_criteria.text: Proposed history and reproducibility tests: also withhold a changed forcing history, such as startup followed by reversal, so that success cannot rest solely on transfer between geometries under similar histories. Repeat experiments with independently prepared samples and, where feasible, independent laboratories. Release the inference protocol, frozen model, solver settings and sufficient data to reproduce the predictions and evaluate uncertainty. These conditions extend the demonstrated idea of transfer without retraining into a proposed experimental validation program.
completion_criteria.label: Changed forcing histories validate transfer with reproducible experiments and predictions

completion_criteria.text: Proposed interpretation of success: report the material classes, histories, geometries and parameter ranges actually passed, together with failures and the boundary of reliable prediction. Passing finite tests would establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions. It would not prove literal universality, unique identification among all constitutive laws or automatic applicability to every yielding, active, particulate or topologically constrained material.
completion_criteria.label: Report tested predictive scope, failures and reliable prediction boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: RHE-02, a theory of amorphous yielding, concerns predicting yield stress and brittle versus ductile failure; RHE-03 concerns a continuum law for dense particulate flow from creep to inertia. Either could supply constitutive mechanisms that a transferable closure must represent. RHE-01 asks whether the resulting material description remains predictive when kinematics and history change. A yield-stress or suspension benchmark can connect these problems without resolving the distinct physics targeted by RHE-02 or RHE-03.

Roster-based synthesis: RHE-04, inverse molecular design of nonlinear polymer-melt rheology, asks which molecular architecture produces a desired response. RHE-01 instead asks whether a given material's inferred stress relation predicts new flows. A transferable forward model could support inverse design, but it would not itself establish a reliable architecture-to-response design procedure. RHE-11, topology-based ring-polymer rheology, supplies another distinct mechanism: ring topology and threaded states may require internal variables beyond those sufficient for other polymers.

Roster-based synthesis: RHE-05 concerns a constitutive theory of active stress that can be inverted for a mechanical task, while RHE-06 concerns addressable solid–fluid switching that persists without a sustaining field or settling particles. Both may require predictive stress descriptions, but active stress generation and persistent switching are additional physical capabilities. Transfer across imposed flows alone would not establish either one.

Roster-based synthesis: RHE-07 seeks local three-dimensional stress measurement without assuming a constitutive law; that could provide independent validation data for RHE-01. RHE-09 seeks computation at the elasticity of real processing; it addresses whether a specified law can be solved accurately and practically. A correct transferable closure and a capable numerical method are complementary requirements, and success at one does not establish the other.

Roster-based synthesis: RHE-08 concerns elasto-inertial turbulence and the drag-reduction ceiling, where constitutive behavior interacts with flow instability and turbulent dynamics. RHE-10 concerns magma containing crystals and bubbles, which adds multiphase material mechanisms. Transferable closures could contribute to both, but transfer demonstrated in the supplied synthetic examples does not establish turbulent predictions or a crystal–bubble magma law.

Historical comparison from the supplied research: a proposed single equation for every complex fluid would encompass this transfer problem while also requiring the distinct mechanisms represented elsewhere in the roster. That broad aspiration helps locate RHE-01 but does not expand its completion criteria to universal rheology. The historical item's full description was not supplied, and the numbered comparisons above are interpretations of the supplied roster titles rather than verified comparisons of complete concept records.

brief.title: Reliable predictions of how complex liquids flow
possible: Engineers could predict how a liquid moves through a new nozzle or coating system without fitting its material model again. The model would predict stress—the internal forces caused by deformation—even when the liquid encounters unfamiliar combinations of sliding, stretching and changes over time.
why: Different material models can match the same simple laboratory tests yet disagree in practical flows. A model that keeps working in unfamiliar conditions could reduce repeated calibration and equipment trials in processing and printing.

sources.showed: This review discusses continuing challenges in mathematical descriptions of fluid behavior.
sources.cited_for: It provides context on continuing challenges in predicting complex-fluid behavior.
sources.not_established: It does not establish a material model experimentally validated across unfamiliar flows and deformation histories.

sources.who: Alp M. Sunol, James V. Roggeveen and collaborators
sources.showed: They learned material models from simulated flow measurements and used them in unfamiliar geometries without retraining. Their models included memory of earlier deformation.
sources.quote: Unlike coordinate-dependent methods, learning local material response enables accurate flow predictions in unseen geometries and conditions without retraining.
sources.cited_for: It demonstrates transfer between simulated flows, including a material model with memory.
sources.not_established: Simulated transfer does not establish reliable predictions across experimentally measured flows and changed deformation histories.

sources.who: Alp M. Sunol, James V. Roggeveen and collaborators

sources.showed: This editorial discusses continuing challenges in describing and predicting complex-fluid behavior.
sources.cited_for: It provides context on unresolved material-model challenges.
sources.not_established: It does not establish a material model experimentally validated across unfamiliar flows and deformation histories.

shown: In a preprint, Sunol and colleagues report that a model learned in a simulated narrowing channel predicted behavior in a cavity driven by a moving wall, without retraining. It also predicted how polymer deformation changed over time. This demonstrates transfer with memory, but uses synthetic flow data.
missing: Experiments have yet to establish reliable predictions in unfamiliar flows with models and parameters held fixed.
Models still need to capture broader forms of memory, including materials whose structure rebuilds or changes with age.
Validation must extend to fully three-dimensional flows and separate material-model errors from measurement and simulation errors.

milestones.label: Fixed models predict unfamiliar flows across three different fluids
milestones.explanation: Fixed material models would have to predict withheld flow speeds and pressure drops for a polymer fluid, a gel and a suspension whose structure changes with flow. This would test transfer across distinct material behaviors.

milestones.label: Predictions meet advance criteria for extra pressure
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to meet criteria set in advance, including the direction and size of measurable extra pressure from spring-like fluid behavior relative to a defined reference. This would make success distinguishable from a loose fit.

milestones.label: Changed flow histories produce reproducible predictions
milestones.explanation: Fixed models would have to predict withheld changes such as flow reversal, with repeat experiments on independently prepared samples and reproducible methods and data. This would test memory beyond a change of geometry.

milestones.label: Tests establish where predictions succeed and fail
milestones.explanation: Results would have to report the materials, histories, geometries and operating ranges that passed, alongside failures and reliability boundaries. This would establish useful scope without claiming universal prediction.

uncertain: Can limited measurements distinguish material models well enough to predict unfamiliar flows?
Which materials, operating ranges and error tolerances would make a convincing experimental benchmark?
How much deformation history must a model retain to predict a material's future response?
